metadata.description: large social network: concurrent read scaling under a production-shaped read/write MIX (paired control vs mixed arms, server-PID sampled)

notes: OVER-THE-WIRE CONCURRENCY LADDER (8 rungs × 2 arm(s) over 1,2,4,8 against 'socialdb'): the headline is whether SERVER-PID CPU scales with C — reads spreading across cores (reader pool #336/#543) vs a single-thread ceiling — measured under a PRODUCTION-SHAPED MIX (reads served while writes commit underneath), not against a frozen graph. The in-process battery this replaces measured the DRIVER, not the server (a ~1-core artifact).

TWO LAYERS OF TRUTH, never conflated (rmp #714, #715). READ: throughput.* is ONE coherent set — the 1500 reads of the best 'mixed' rung (C=8), at 1428.4 ops/s, and throughput.abort_rate = 0.000000 is the READ abort rate. It is a MEASURED zero, not a placeholder: a standalone auto-commit read runs at SNAPSHOT ISOLATION (rmp #543/#545), so it can neither abort a writer nor be aborted by one — that is invariant I1, and the run FAILS if a read ever aborts. WRITE: the writers' evidence lives in the workload map and is split in two. ENGINE: 0 of 1648 transaction attempts were aborted by SSI (engine_abort_rate 0.000000). APPLICATION: 1648 of 1648 business units COMMITTED (write_commit_rate 1.000000), at 0.0000 retries per commit, 0 exhausting their retry budget. A high engine abort rate WITH a full application commit rate is a HEALTHY system under contention: the application-visible cost of contention is LATENCY (see write_p99_ms, which is RETRY-INCLUSIVE), not lost work.

THE COST OF THE MIX (rmp #714). Every rung was run TWICE, back to back, same concurrency, same op budget, same graph: once with the writers OFF (the control) and once with them ON (the treatment — the production-shaped default this report headlines). What the mix costs the READ path: -0.2% at the best rung (C=8). Rung by rung: C=1: 263.3 → 215.4 ops/s (-18.2%), p99 14.7 → 31.7 ms | C=2: 344.6 → 260.8 ops/s (-24.3%), p99 36.5 → 42.5 ms | C=4: 871.2 → 866.7 ops/s (-0.5%), p99 19.8 → 20.2 ms | C=8: 1430.7 → 1428.4 ops/s (-0.2%), p99 29.1 → 29.3 ms. The control arm runs FIRST at every rung, so it warms the buffer pool for the mixed arm — the cost reported here is therefore a conservative LOWER BOUND. This is the number a capacity planner needs and that a read-only ladder against a frozen graph can never produce.

THE WRITE STREAM is production-shaped, not a storm: 2 writer(s) paced at one business unit every 20ms, each driven through MANAGED RETRY (bounded exponential backoff + jitter — what session.execute_write does in every official driver). 25% of the units are a read-modify-write of one of 4 TRENDING articles (`SET a.hot = coalesce(a.hot,0)+1`); the rest touch a random user's `registered` timestamp. The hot component is what makes SSI — and therefore the retry path — LOAD-BEARING: a purely random write stream conflicts with nobody, aborts nothing, and leaves the retry path as dead code and the bounded-retries invariant vacuous.

SLOW-READER PROBE (invariant I5, the GC pin — rmp #551): while 204 heavy 'top_liked' reads (p50 14.7ms, max 18.4ms) held their MVCC snapshots open for 3.0s, the writers committed 271 of 271 business units underneath them (0 engine aborts). A long reader pins the GC watermark; if that pin could stall the write path, this window would show ZERO commits — and the ladder, whose reads are mostly short, would never have noticed.

KNEE: VERDICT: reads SCALED ACROSS CORES — 17 threads were busy and total core usage reached 6.42, well above any single thread's 0.45. The read path spread work across cores (the off-thread reader pool #336/#543 is engaged).
KNEE: Server disk read IO at the top rung: 0.0 MiB over the rung (low ⇒ served from the buffer pool).

storage.bytes_per_node / bytes_per_relationship are PRESENT and honest even though the mix COMMITTED 1648 business unit(s) into this same store (rmp #711/#714). Both write shapes are property SETs on EXISTING nodes (`u.registered` on a random user, `a.hot` on a trending article): they mutate values, they never create or delete an element. The node/relationship counts therefore still describe exactly the graph this store holds, and the division stays real arithmetic over the right graph. The figure does now include the durable cost of the `hot` property the mix added to the 4 trending article(s) — a genuine, measured part of this store's footprint.

SERVER ON-DISK FOOTPRINT (local, co-located), measured directly from the server's store directory and DECOMPOSED — a lumped total would blend bytes that scale with the graph with bytes that do not: data image (graphus.store) 4.5MiB | doublewrite buffers (graphus.dwb) 16.9MiB | redo log (graphus.wal/seg.<lsn>) 19.2MiB | catalog/locks 0.0MiB.

STORAGE EFFICIENCY: the redo log RETAINS 19.2MiB on disk = 4.3x the 4.5MiB data image it protects, having WRITTEN 48.3MiB of cumulative redo over the run — so 29.2MiB (60%) was RECYCLED, not accumulated. The Mode A bulk-load's redo is reclaimed at load end (`rmp` #579) and the WAL segment target is sized to the store (`rmp` #706), so sealed segments below the checkpoint floor are freed instead of retained; what remains is the recent redo tail, not the whole log (before those fixes the same workload held ~9.3x and grew monotonically, `rmp` #702). The doublewrite buffers are a FIXED preallocation (16.9MiB total, one per database, independent of graph size), so on a small graph they dominate the footprint while on a large one they amortise to nothing.

SPACE AMPLIFICATION: the DATA image is 2.48x the 1.8MiB logical graph (the generator's CSV bytes) — this is the ratio that scales with the graph. Counting every durable byte (data + doublewrite + WAL = 40.6MiB) the whole directory is 22.56x logical, but that figure is dominated by the two constant-cost items above and must not be read as a per-byte storage cost.
